description: "Ready for liftoff! We are building an interactive Space Mission Game powered by real NASA data. Our goal is to let players plan, launch, and navigate authentic space missions while keeping the gameplay fun and easy to pick up. We are looking for teammates who love game design, 2D/3D art, coding, sound, or space science to help us build a playable prototype!"
summary: Mission Control: Beyond the Unknown – Dilmun-1 is an educational space mission design game inspired by NASA’s Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players take the role of mission planners and design spacecraft for three missions: exploring the Moon, travelling to Mars, and repairing the International Space Station (ISS). They must balance a $600 million budget, spacecraft mass, power requirements, communications, fuel and scientific instruments. Players then launch, dock, manage mission challenges, land and complete scientific objectives. The game incorporates NASA educational resources and live NASA data feeds, including solar activity from DONKI and near-Earth asteroid information from NASA’s API. By combining interactive gameplay with real space science concepts, the project makes complex mission-planning principles more accessible and encourages students to explore STEM subjects.
details:
Project Overview

Mission Control: Beyond the Unknown – Dilmun-1 is an interactive educational space mission design game created for NASA's Space Apps Challenge. Our project aims to make space exploration and mission planning more engaging by allowing players to take the role of mission planners and experience the decisions involved in designing and operating space missions.

How the Game Works

Players can choose between three missions:

  • Dilmun-L – Lunar Explorer: Travel to the Moon, manage astronauts' suit oxygen and complete a rover expedition towards the lunar north pole.
  • Dilmun-1 – Mars Pathfinder: Undertake a long journey to Mars, manage emergencies and radiation challenges, land safely and explore the Martian surface.
  • Dilmun-R – ISS Repair: Dock with the International Space Station and repair essential systems, including its cooling, electrical power and air systems.

Before launching, players design their spacecraft by selecting a launch vehicle, crew module, power system, communication antenna, propellant reserve and scientific instruments. They must stay within a $600 million budget while ensuring that the spacecraft's mass does not exceed the rocket's capacity and that its power supply meets its requirements.

Players then experience different mission stages, including rocket launches, orbital rendezvous and docking, deep-space travel, emergency management, powered descent and surface exploration. Their decisions and ability to manage challenges influence mission success.

NASA Resources and Scientific Data

The project incorporates NASA educational and technical resources to make its missions and scientific concepts more realistic. These include NASA's Design and Develop Science Missions guide, GMAT resources, Goddard's Mission Design Lab, JPL's Concept Maturity Levels, NASA Mission Visualization and CubeSat 101.

The Learning Center introduces important space engineering concepts such as delta-v, gravity turns, solar flux, radioisotope power systems (RTGs), communication link budgets and powered descent. It also uses examples from real NASA missions, including Apollo, Perseverance, Curiosity and the International Space Station.

The game also incorporates NASA's open-data APIs. The DONKI API provides solar-flare information relevant to in-game radiation challenges, while NASA's Near Earth Object API provides information about near-Earth asteroids. Built-in data snapshots allow the game to retain relevant information when live data is unavailable.

Tools and Development

The game is built as a browser-based application using HTML, CSS and JavaScript. These technologies provide its structure, visual interface, gameplay mechanics, spacecraft calculations and interactive features. HTML Canvas is used for animated scenes and visual simulations, Web Audio provides sound effects, and browser local storage saves mission progress and records.

AI-assisted tools supported parts of the development process, including coding, visual and audio assets, and working with NASA's educational resources and datasets. Our team shaped the project's concept, mission ideas and overall direction, bringing these elements together into a single interactive experience.

Creativity, Benefits and Intended Impact

The project's creativity lies in combining spacecraft design, mission management, scientific challenges, educational explanations and NASA data within one game. Instead of simply reading about space exploration, players experience the engineering decisions and trade-offs involved in planning a mission.

The project also incorporates Bahrain's identity through the Dilmun name, Bahraini mission control and the concept of a Bahraini astronaut exploring space.

Our intended impact is to make space science and engineering more accessible and engaging for students, encourage interest in STEM subjects and help players understand the complexity of planning real space missions.

The game uses simplified educational models and is an independent student project, not an official NASA product.
